div.p: The formal verification of task schedulability is getting more important in the automotive domain as more and more applications are integrated into domain specific con trollers. Especially for safety critical applications an indepth knowledge about the worst-case response time of tasks is of utmost importance. Such systems often consist of subsystems that comprise of a collection of tasks, called transactions, which are triggered by external events. We adapt a well known response time analysis to analyze asynchronous task sets where subsets may be triggered from different clock references. Therefore we refine the original computational model from the literature to capture the information about transaction clock references. To determine the schedulability of the system we first analyze all task subsets which are triggered by the same clock reference.

Then we combine the results to derive the response times for the complete task set. The approach incorporates no overestimation of the response times and therefore represets a necessary and sufficient schedulability test for such systems. The computational complexity of the presented approach is O(nm) with n being the number of tasks and m the number of clock references in the system. We apply the analysis to a real-world scenario from the automotive safety domain to confirm the computational feasibility and validity of the analysis in real-world systems.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In future premium class automobiles the number of active and passive safety applications that have tight constraints in terms of timing will be rapidly increasing. This is because new remote sensing devices offer perception capabilities that enable a vehicle to interact in a context sensitive manner and thereby increase safety for both passengers and vulnerable road users. Especially active safety applications, like autonomous emer gency brakes, airbag pre-conditioning, reversible belt tension ers, operate in a distributed way and have high requirements in terms of signal delay from sensor to actuator. Generally speaking a higher signal delay results in reduced application performance.

New time-triggered control paradigms offer means to design distributed systems that have deterministic timing behavior and low signal delay and signal jitter [4]. However, deterministic system timing requires the task-set of a time-triggered ECU to meet hard real-time requirements. In traditional time-triggered real-time systems meeting predefined deadlines is validated by investigating the task schedule which is created offline during the design phase. When legacy subsystems are involved, which is usually the case in the automotive safety domain, parts 978-1-4244-7125-6/10/$26.00 ©20 10 IEEE of the system may not be implemented in a purely time triggered manner, hence, formal verification from reactive system engineering has to be applied.

The challenge is to combine classical fixed-priority pre emptive scheduling with time-triggered deterministic system behavior. Also, tight economical constraints must not be neglected. Therefore, overestimation of the computational re quirements of the real-time system has to be kept low. In this paper we use and refine a well known formal verification method and apply it to a real-world example from the automo tive domain. The system we investigate incorporates a passive airbag application and new active applications which are hosted on the same ECU as the passive applications. The next section introduces to the area of response time analysis (RTA) and discusses different approaches. In section III we define our computational model for single clock systems and revise the original RTA method from the literature. Section IV proposes an extended computational model and an adaptation of the RTA for multiple clock systems. An analysis of performance aspects of the RTA is provided in the case study in section V. Eventually, we conclude this paper in section VI.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: The discipline of real-time system design and analysis has an extensive history and produced many important results over the past decades. In terms of schedulability analysis the seminal work of Lyu and Layland [7] needs to be mentioned as well as one of the starting point for fixed-priority pre emptive scheduling analysis proposed by Tindell [13]. Tindell formalized the schedulability problem for fixed-priority pre emptive synchronous task sets and later extended his own work to account for asynchronous task sets. In synchronous task sets all tasks are activated at the same instant and re-activated according to their activation period. Finding the critical instant for synchronous task sets is easy, Le. the instant when all tasks are activated at the same time. However, finding the critical instant for asynchronous task sets, where tasks may contain activation offsets is proven to be co-NP-complete [2]. Hence, pseudo-polynomial solutions that contain a certain amount of pessimism have been developed in [12].

In this paper we propose an RTA algorithm that utilizes the formulae proposed by Tindell. We use a different computa-tional model than used in the original analysis which helps us to cope with the complexity and enables us to calculate exact solutions. As the problem we solve is co-N"P-complete, the theoretical complexity of the proposed exact algorithm is computationally infeasible. However, since application specific constraints and the different computational model compared to [12], [2], [8] exclude most of the instants one has to analyze using the original approach by Tindell, the actual complexity is much smaller and in many cases manageable.

Different approaches to response-time analysis have been proposed in [9], [1] and [11]. In all articles task activations are regarded as streams, or flows, of events and response times are resolved by evaluating (potentially combined) event streams and service curves that correspond to the shared computation device. Although these methods do not suffer from the computational complexity of the approach considered in this work, the computational model used in the event flow representation of the real-time system is different from the one used in this paper. Event stream models describe worst case activation schemes triggered by multiple external clocks. Hence, periodic event streams without activation jitter may be activated at arbitrary points in time. Therefore, the same over estimation of the response-times as observed in [10] would have to be expected using event stream models. Note that this is not caused by poor analysis techniques but by the different computational model.

In our approach we cope with multiple time references by following a two step approach. In step one all tasks triggered by the same clock reference are analyzed. As we will show this can be done efficiently when taking domain specific constraints into account. In step two we combine the results from step one to solve the original problem. Step two increases the complexity of the RTA significantly, however, for automotive systems exact solutions even for large task sets can be obtained.

div.head: III. RESPON SE TI ME ANALY SI S FOR SINGLE CLOCK REFERENCE SYSTEMS
div.p: In this section we introduce the computational model used in our analysis for single clock reference systems. We present the starting point of the RTA developed by Tindell in [12]. We adapt the RTA to account for application specific constraints which enables us to obtain exact results for single time reference task subsets. In the next section we combine the results from the single clock reference systems to solve the multi time reference problem.

div.head: B. Analysis Using Offset Information
div.p: The response time of a task can be calculated taking into account the properties of the task itself and the properties of all higher priority tasks which may be pre-empted over the task under analysis. The central concept to do such an analysis taking into account task offsets 0 is by deriving so-called busy windows which were introduced in [6]. A busy window is a period of time in which a processor is not idle at any time. Clearly, with pre-emptive scheduling the task with the lowest priority is always finished at the end of a busy period. The critical instant is the point in time that precedes the busy window resulting in the longest response time for the analyzed task.

div.head: IV. RESPON SE TI ME ANALY SI S FOR MULTIPLE CLOCK REFERENCE SYSTEMS
div.p: In the previous section we investigated the WCRT analysis for systems consisting of one global clock reference that triggers all transactions. In this section we cover the analysis of systems that consists of multiple clock references. The original computational model lacks the information required to determine the clock reference of each transaction, therefore, we first have to refine the computational model to capture this additional information. The analysis contexts for each transaction set which belong to the same clock reference are created using the procedure in the previous section. After the analysis contexts for each single clock transaction set have been created, we have to merge them into one joint set of analysis contexts. To do so, we consider each single clock transaction set as one transaction with period equals to the hyper-period of the transaction set. In real-world scenarios the RTA is feasible if the number of different clock references is small. In the following we will show such a real-world scenario.

div.head: V. SYSTEM ANALY SI S
div.p: In the previous section we proposed procedures to create the analysis context for systems with single and multiple clock references. Using the formulae from the original analysis the WCRT of all tasks can be computed by evaluating all analysis contexts and remembering the one that led to the critical instant. As we only investigate task activation schemes which may occur in reality the WCRT includes no overestimation of the actual WCRT, i.e. the analysis is exact. Consider the following active/passive safety system.

div.head: A. Automotive Safety Architecture
div.p: The safety architecture in figure 4 consists of an integrated safety ECU which receives input from different sources. A forward looking sensor device perceives the current driving scene and triggers active safety applications and pedestrian protection via an event-triggered bus. A time-triggered task is triggered at a specific instant when the time-triggered bus is in a specific state. The communication via the time-triggered bus is also triggered by the clock of the bus. An external watchdog participates in a challenge/response mechanism. In the safety ECU a sanity check is performed upon this request. Moreover, a traditional legacy subsystem for airbag deployment is triggered periodically by its respective sensor ICs.

The legacy subsystem consists of a number of periodic tasks responsible for the generation of features from the sensor data upon which a decision is made regarding whether or not the airbag needs to be deployed. Also the basic diagnosis function ality is implemented in the legacy subsystem. The active and pedestrian safety applications and the ECU sanity check are triggered event-based with a certain miminum interarrival time (MINT). The time-triggered tasks are activated periodically but the activation period is subject to drift, as the ECU and the time-triggered bus do not share the same global clock. All tasks of the embedded software system and their respective real-time properties are summarized in table II.

div.head: B. Timing Analysis
div.p: We analysed the system in figure 4 using two different approaches. First, we applyied the simulation model presented in [5] to analyze the system from an average case perspective. Using statistical modeling and simulation is feasible in clock drifts between elements have to be considered. However, investigating the worst-case timing using statistical simulation is difficult because very long simulation durations would be neccessary. On the other hand, the simulation provides knowledge about mean response times and average controller load.

The simulation is performed repeatedly until a predefined confidence threshold is reached. Between each simlation repli cation the clock drifts and initial transaction phase is evaluated statistically and changed. By doing so we create random samples of the mean and max response times of all tasks. Using the samples from each replication we create the box plots of the mean task response times depicted in figure 5. The top and the bottom of the box which contains the thick horizontal bar represent the 75% quartile and the 25% quartile, i.e. the latency bound which 75%/25% of the replication instances did not exceed. The thicker line inside of the box presents the median of the values. The whiskers with the bars at the end of the line represent the data point that exceed the quartiles, but are limited to 1.5 x IQR, IQR being the inter quartile range. Outlier are represented by circles.

The confidence factor of the mean task response times was set to accept a relative error of 5% with the probability of 95%. Over all simulation replications the simulated WCRT of all tasks is depicted in figure 6. The WCRTs of the tasks is not

The red crosses in figure 6 represent the calculated WCRTs using the RTA presented in section IV. Two important findings can be observed in the figure :
1) Even through extensive simulation the maximum re sponse time from the simulation may be significantly lower than the calculated WCRT. 2) The maximum response time in the simulation does not exceed the calculated WCRT.

The RTA provides important information regarding the worst-case behavior of the system by providing upper bounds of the WCRT of all real-time tasks. Especially for the lower priority tasks the gap between WCRT and maximum response time during the simulation runs can be significant. In the above mentioned system the number of analysis contexts for the lowest priority task summed up to 1272. The RTA calculates the respective WCRT in a matter of seconds and can handle systems of up to millions of analysis contexts. However, for very large systems with many different clock references and high amount of transaction per clock reference, the presented RTA will not be feasible. For these systems heuristics have to be found that calculate tight upper bounds to the WCRT without compromizing the computational feasiblity.

div.head: VI. CONCLU SION S
div.p: In the presented work we applied the well known RTA approach from Tindell to automotive real-time systems. The original approach considers each transaction of tasks to be triggered by its individual external clock reference. Thus, each transaction may be activated at arbitrary points in time leading to worst-case scenarios that might not be possible in systems where subsets of the task-set are triggered by the same clock reference. Such systems are usually present in the automotive safety domain.

We use a refined computational model to account for auto motive specific constraints and the above mentioned multiple clock reference situation. The computational model includes information regarding the clock reference each transaction is triggered by. Using this additional information we perform a two step analysis to calculate the WCRTs of the complete task set. First, we investigate all tasks triggered by the same clock reference. For n tasks this can be done in O( n) as the number of instants we need to check is influenced only by the hyper-period of the task-subset. Second, we combine the results from the frist step by considering the subsets as individual transactions and using the original RTA approach and recombine each task activation from the transactions with oneanother. The second step increases the complexity to O(nm) with m being the number of clock references.

Despite its high computational complexity the analysis is applicable in automotive systems with relatively short schedule lengths, or hyper-periods, and limited number of different clock references. We highlighted the the strength of the analysis by applying it to a system architecture from the automotive safety domain and deriving WCRTs of the tasks which are otherwise difficult to determine. As the analysis calculates exact results with no overestimation of the response times, highly efficient software systems can emerge.

A. Extended Computational ModelThe system model introduced in section III-A defines one global clock c that triggers all transactions. We replace the single clock reference by a set of clock references C, hence, S = (T, R, C). The model of the transactions is refined accordingly. Each transaction j E R consists of a tuple (Tj, Cj) with Cj E C. B. Multiple Time References With the refined computational model we can extend the existing RTA for single clock reference systems to account for multiple clock references. Again, our main task is to find the critical instant but unlike in the single clock reference scenario we have to treat transactions triggered by different clock references different to transactions triggered by the same clock reference. Consider figure 3. Transactions 0,1, and 2 are triggered by the same clock reference and transaction 3 and 4 are triggered by a different clock reference. The analysis contexts for the RTA transactions 0, 1, and 2 have to conform to the activation schemes as described in section III. The same is true for transactions 3 and 4. Unlike in the single clock reference system tasks which are triggered by different clock references are subject to clock drift. The clock drift of the transaction triggers results in a constantly changing phase offset between the transactions from different clock references. In other words, transactions for different clock references may be triggered at arbitrary points in time. For the analysis context generation this means assuming any task activation in a transaction has no effects on possible task activations in transactions with different clock reference.
